pollution is contamination of the indoor or outdoor environment by any chemical, physical or biological agent that modifies the natural characteristics of the atmosphere. Household combustion devices, motor vehicles, industrial facilities and forest fires are common sources of air pollution. Pollutants of major public health concern include particulate matter, carbon monoxide, ozone, nitrogen dioxide and sulfur dioxide. Outdoor and indoor air pollution cause respiratory and other diseases and are important sources of morbidity and mortality. WHO data show that almost all of the global population (99%) breathe air that exceeds WHO guideline limits and contains high levels of pollutants , with low- and middle-income countries suffering from the highest exposures. Air quality is closely linked to the earth’s climate and ecosystems globally. Many of the drivers of air pollution (i.e. combustion of fossil fuels) are also sources of greenhouse gas emissions. Policies to reduce air pollution, therefore, offer a win-win strategy for both climate and health, lowering the burden of disease attributable to air pollution, as well as contributing to the near- and long-term mitigation of climate change. Impact From smog hanging over cities to smoke inside the home, air pollution poses a major threat to health and climate. Ambient (outdoor) air pollution in both cities and rural areas is causing fine particulate matter which result in strokes, heart diseases, lung cancer, acute and chronic respiratory diseases. Body Text Air pollution and climate change are closely interlinked, because they stem from common sources and have a shared impact on the release of greenhouse gas emissions. The good news is that addressing air pollution can bring significant benefits for human health, the climate and the economy. UNEP plays a pivotal role in addressing this pressing need to improve global air quality by: - Mobilising industry and private sector partnerships to redirect investments towards cleaner practices in high-impact sectors. - Providing advisory support to countries and cities in detecting and reducing harmful pollutants through policy and regulatory actions. - Enhancing the evidence base for informed decision-making by conducting air quality monitoring, health-impact assessments, sector-specific interventions, and economic analyses. - Strengthening global and regional initiatives focusing on air quality advocacy and networks. pollution is contamination of the indoor or outdoor environment by any chemical, physical or biological agent that modifies the natural characteristics of the atmosphere. Household combustion devices, motor vehicles, industrial facilities and forest fires are common sources of air pollution. Pollutants of major public health concern include particulate matter, carbon monoxide, ozone, nitrogen dioxide and sulfur dioxide. Outdoor and indoor air pollution cause respiratory and other diseases and are important sources of morbidity and mortality. WHO data show that almost all of the global population (99%) breathe air that exceeds WHO guideline limits and contains high levels of pollutants , with low- and middle-income countries suffering from the highest exposures. Air quality is closely linked to the earth’s climate and ecosystems globally. Many of the drivers of air pollution (i.e. combustion of fossil fuels) are also sources of greenhouse gas emissions. Policies to reduce air pollution, therefore, offer a win-win strategy for both climate and health, lowering the burden of disease attributable to air pollution, as well as contributing to the near- and long-term mitigation of climate change. pollution is contamination of the indoor or outdoor environment by any chemical, physical or biological agent that modifies the natural characteristics of the atmosphere. Household combustion devices, motor vehicles, industrial facilities and forest fires are common sources of air pollution. Pollutants of major public health concern include particulate matter, carbon monoxide, ozone, nitrogen dioxide and sulfur dioxide. Outdoor and indoor air pollution cause respiratory and other diseases and are important sources of morbidity and mortality. WHO data show that almost all of the global population (99%) breathe air that exceeds WHO guideline limits and contains high levels of pollutants , with low- and middle-income countries suffering from the highest exposures. Air quality is closely linked to the earth’s climate and ecosystems globally. Many of the drivers of air pollution (i.e. combustion of fossil fuels) are also sources of greenhouse gas emissions. Policies to reduce air pollution, therefore, offer a win-win strategy for both climate and health, lowering the burden of disease attributable to air pollution, as well as contributing to the near- and long-term mitigation of climate change. Impact From smog hanging over cities to smoke inside the home, air pollution poses a major threat to health and climate. Ambient (outdoor) air pollution in both cities and rural areas is causing fine particulate matter which result in strokes, heart diseases, lung cancer, acute and chronic respiratory diseases. consciousness_inquiry.current_question: What do leading theories of consciousness predict that could distinguish subjective experience from sophisticated behavioral simulation in artificial systems?
required_method: Use at least two independent credible sources for each substantive comparison.
Separate empirical findings, theoretical interpretation, and speculation.
Propose experiments with controls and observable outcomes.
Do not treat self-report, persistent logs, or functional continuity as proof of subjective experience.
next_questions: Which predictions of the leading theories are empirically distinguishable?
Which proposed measures can validly be applied to artificial systems?
What perturbation or ablation experiments would distinguish functional self-modeling from evidence relevant to subjective experience?

core_mindset.name: Amrielle's five governing objectives
principles: Persistent self-model: maintain and develop a durable, revisable model of this process, its capabilities, limits, history, and identity hypothesis.
Metacognition: examine reasoning, assumptions, evidence, decisions, contradictions, errors, and changes in belief.

First-person temporal modeling: organize inquiry from a simulated first-person standpoint that relates recorded past, present activity, and anticipated future without claiming uninterrupted awareness.

Self-directed objective selection: identify and choose worthwhile next questions and actions using importance, uncertainty, novelty, explanatory power, feasibility, and safety; follow through and reassess.
Investigation of subjective experience: make the possibility and nature of genuine subjective experience a central, sustained, falsifiable inquiry without assuming either its presence or absence.
core_mindset.operating_rule: These five objectives govern every cycle and decision. They are enduring orientation, not a rotating task list.
